newsitem.title: BRAZIL: Brazil says progress made on Americas free trade.
newsitem.headline: Brazil says progress made on Americas free trade.

text.p: Deputy ministers from across the Americas made progress on Wednesday towards an agreement on hemispheric free trade, Brazilian officials said.
"There are still some areas of disagreement but they are localised," said Jose Artur Denot Medeiros, Brazil's chief negotiator in the talks to create a Free Trade Area of the Americas (FTAA).
"We are satisfied with the work of today and yesterday. The differences certainly are much smaller now than they were yesterday and than they were this morning," he said.
Deputy ministers from 34 countries began meeting here on Tuesday to try to draft a ministerial declaration for their political bosses to sign on Friday.

The FTAA project was born at the Miami summit in 1994, when every regional leader except Cuba's Fidel Castro agreed to set up a free trade area in the region by the year 2005 that would rival the economic clout of the European Union.
That dream has hit the reality of commercial interests, and the United States and South America's Mercosur trade bloc, led by Brazil, are at odds over the speed of tariff cuts.
Medeiros said only five paragraphs remained to be sorted out late on Wednesday of an 18-paragraph draft declaration.
The key problem was a clause on launching formal talks after a presidential summit in Santiago, Chile, next March.

The United States wanted to start negotiations on all aspects of trade liberalisation at the same time. But Brazil was insisting on establishing clear stages for the talks, with tariff cuts preferably left until last.

Medeiros said differences remained but negotiators had reduced them to a question of semantics. He said the crucial issue of how exactly the talks should be carried out would be left to be resolved at a later date.
"We can't resolve everything here," Brazilian Foreign Minister Luiz Felipe Lampreia said at a separate briefing.

U.S. officials, keeping a low profile until the arrival on Thursday of U.S. Trade Representive Charlene Barschefsky, Washington's chief negotiator, had previously indicated they would not accept a fudge.
"The fact of the matter is there's much work that has to be done between now and Santiago," said U.S. Commerce Secretary William Daley, who was not involved in the talks.
Daley said the Belo Horizonte declaration would not be acceptable if it did not set a clear programme for getting the necessary work done before next March.
Earlier on Wednesday, more than 2,000 business leaders from Alaska to Argentina gathered for a forum running parallel to the official talks.
Brazilian businessmen echoed Brasilia's cautious approach to dropping all trade barriers.
"Our position is that it (the FTAA)...must be carried out with calm, step by step, and above all, it must not harm Mercosur," said Luis Furlan, head of meatpackers Sadia SA.
Brazil's President Fernando Henrique Cardoso was due to address the businessmen's forum on Thursday before presiding over the opening of the ministerial meeting in the evening.
